## Abstract

Data-driven dynamical models are increasingly fitted to walking, yet gait dynamics are still most often summarized by asymptotic stability, which says whether a disturbance eventually dies out but little about how walking responds in the meantime. The size and duration of a disturbance, the movements that compensate for it, and the course of recovery can differ even when long-term stability is similar. Non-normal dynamics can amplify disturbances before they decay, while active control and repeated forcing shape the response observed during walking. Floquet multipliers summarize only part of that behavior and are difficult to estimate reliably from short, noisy recordings. We argue for models that describe the evolving gait dynamics and predict meaningful departures from ordinary walking. We identify six requirements: useful response predictions, credible sustained behavior, reproducibility, practical performance with realistic recordings, interpretable dynamical structure, and comparability across people and conditions. Comparisons on oscillators, a walking template, and human gait support linear models in delay coordinates as a strong practical foundation across these requirements. Nonlinear models can predict particular recoveries more accurately; the case for linear models rests on their combined strengths and the tools available to examine their responses. Appropriate perturbation data and independent validation remain essential. A model that reproduces the gait cycle has not yet demonstrated that it captures how walking responds and recovers.

## What do we need to understand about walking?

Walking is a rhythm produced by interacting body mechanics, neural control, and the environment, and it is disturbed and corrected at every stride. Data-driven dynamical models are increasingly used to learn that behaviour from movement recordings. What should such a model capture? Describing ordinary walking, its average pattern or its eventual return to that pattern, is not enough. The questions concern how walking changes over time after a disturbance: the size and duration of an excursion, the joints and limbs involved, and how their coordination evolves during recovery.

Three traditions describe this behaviour. Mechanistic templates and musculoskeletal simulations represent the interactions explicitly, but fitting them to individuals and predicting changes in kinematics remain difficult [@winner2023]. Stability and variability measures offer compact descriptions computed from movement recordings [@dingwell2000; @dingwell2006; @bruijn2013]. Each reads one part of the response to a disturbance (@fig-schematic B): a short-term Lyapunov exponent its early rate of divergence, a Floquet multiplier its late rate of return. Neither describes how large the response becomes, when, or which movements carry it, and systems that share one or both numbers can respond differently (@fig-schematic C). The margin of stability evaluates the state at a single instant relative to the base of support [@hof2005] and so describes no response at all. Data-driven dynamical models provide another route: learning how observed movements evolve, from linear step-to-step maps to nonlinear sequence models [@revzen2012; @winner2023].

The value of a model is whether it helps answer questions about that evolution. Reconstructing ordinary strides accurately is useful, but does not establish how an individual responds to a disturbance. Likewise, a stability number does not describe which movements compensate, how large an excursion becomes, or how long recovery takes.

We first explain why asymptotic stability is an inadequate primary target, both conceptually and in its practical estimation. We then define what a useful gait model should provide and compare modeling approaches against those needs. Linear models offer a particularly useful combination of reproducibility, tractability, and accessible dynamical analysis. Their promise is a broader description of walking and recovery, with predictions and interpretations that can be tested (@fig-schematic A).

![**What stability measures read from the response to a disturbance, and what they miss.** Exact responses of small linear systems, time in strides; no fitting. (A) The argument of this paper. (B) The size of one response relative to the disturbance (root-mean-square over disturbance directions). A short-term Lyapunov exponent summarizes its early rate of divergence, typically over the first stride; a Floquet multiplier, its late rate of return per stride once the slowest response dominates (dashed, parallel to the late response). The transient structure is the whole response: its growth, peak, timing and duration, and, with more than one movement, which movements carry it. In walking, the next disturbance arrives within about a stride (@fig-transient). (C) Three pairs of systems. The first pair shares its multiplier, the second its early rate, and the third both; only the whole response separates all three.](figures/Figure_01){#fig-schematic fig-alt="An overview of the paper's argument; one response to a disturbance with the windows read by a Lyapunov exponent and a Floquet multiplier; and three pairs of response curves with a table of which measures tell each pair apart."}

## Why asymptotic stability is not the right primary target

### A long-term return rate does not describe the recovery that matters

Floquet multipliers characterize whether sufficiently small deviations from a periodic orbit eventually shrink and their asymptotic rates of change per cycle. This makes them a natural measure of local gait stability [@dingwell2006], but leaves much of the recovery unspecified.

Walking never settles into the regime that a multiplier describes (@fig-transient). A multiplier gives the rate at which a deviation shrinks once only its slowest component remains, and reaching that regime takes several strides: at the multipliers reported for human walking, about 0.3–0.8 per stride [@dingwell2006; @bruijn2013], a single disturbance needs roughly 2–10 strides to fall to a tenth of its size. Walking is disturbed far more often. Each step's collision with the ground redirects the body's motion [@kuo2005], foot placement is adjusted from step to step [@wang2014; @bruijn2018], and terrain, the body, and neural control add variability throughout the stride. The deviation observed at any moment is therefore a superposition of responses to recent disturbances, most still within their first stride or two. Stride-to-stride variability is a property of these short-time responses rather than of their eventual rate, and the response over the first strides after a disturbance is the behaviour a model must capture.

![**Walking is disturbed again before it recovers, and its short-time response is not what the multiplier predicts.** Ground truth, no fitting; norms in observed coordinates (each variable scaled by its SD along the cycle). Responses use the step map linearized at the gait, so they add exactly; the full simulation differs from the sum by a median of 14%. (B) Within a stride. Coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo (FHN): distance from the cycle after one disturbance, relative to its size; thick, root-mean-square over disturbance directions and the phase at which the disturbance arrives; thin, the worst phase and direction; dashed, the multiplier's prediction. (C) Stride to stride: worst-case growth of the n-stride map from the cycle against the multiplier's prediction ρⁿ (dashed), for coupled FHN and SLIP with feedback (two steps per stride). (D) Share of the observed deviation (stationary variance) contributed by disturbances younger than a given age. Coupled FHN with continuous disturbances of equal size in every variable, one cycle taken as one stride; SLIP with one disturbance per step, with speed feedback and open loop (ρ = 0.95 per step); grey band, a one-dimensional stride map with the multipliers reported for human walking, 1 − ρ^2n^. Shading in B–D, the first cycle or stride. The oscillator family behind B and lasting phase shifts are in @suppfig-oscillators.](figures/Figure_02){#fig-transient fig-alt="Four panels: a SLIP walker's centre-of-mass height with a disturbance at every step and its deviation as the sum of overlapping responses; one disturbance's distance from the cycle in coupled FHN against the multiplier's prediction, within a stride and from stride to stride; and the share of the observed deviation contributed by disturbances younger than a given age."}

A disturbance can grow before it decays. In a non-normal system, interactions between response directions can produce transient amplification even when all transverse multipliers indicate eventual return [@trefethen2005; @hess2026nonnormality]. The direction and phase of the disturbance affect its peak size, its redistribution between movements, and the time course of recovery. The ground-truth examples show growth that the multiplier misses, both within a stride and from one stride to the next (@fig-transient B–C); it appears across a family of oscillators with very different multipliers (@suppfig-oscillators).


Because the observed deviations are responses to ongoing disturbances under active control, they reflect forcing, mechanics, and feedback together. Beyond a local linear approximation, overlapping responses can also interact nonlinearly. An estimated multiplier describes aspects of the combined system and does not separately identify the mechanical plant or neural controller.

Persistent changes in timing and coordination provide further reasons to examine the trajectory. A phase shift can leave a person walking on the same cycle at a different time (@suppfig-oscillators C), while a coordination disturbance changes the relation between movements. Both can matter even when motion remains bounded. The full response is therefore the object of interest; its asymptotic rate is one summary.

### Even the stability number is difficult to recover from gait data

The practical problem compounds the conceptual one. Short recordings contain relatively few independent strides despite many within-stride samples. Measurement noise, the chosen state variables and gait event, and approximation of the dynamics all affect an estimated return map.

The SLIP walking example makes these difficulties concrete (@fig-floquet-maps). More strides reduce scatter without necessarily removing measurement-noise bias. Phase-indexed and piecewise-linear models provide more detailed descriptions within the cycle, but their composed return maps remain sensitive to noise and the partition used. Dividing a stride into more pieces does not by itself resolve the estimation problem.

![**Data-driven Floquet multipliers of SLIP walking are data-hungry and biased by measurement noise; for a linear map the bias is correctable.** Kicked SLIP walks (stride-level kicks at vertical leg orientation, VLO; open loop, truth 0.628 ± 0.713i, ρ = 0.95), 20 walks of 2000 steps; measurement noise is relative to the stride-to-stride SD of each variable. (A) Eigenvalues of the VLO return map from 20 walks: 30 steps with noise 0.25×, and 2000 noise-free steps; star, truth; dotted, unit circle. (B) Estimated spectral radius against record length, noise-free (solid) and with noise 0.25× (dashed); median and interquartile range over walks. More strides reduce the scatter, not the bias; the section map by instrumental variables (IV; previous step as the instrument) removes it. (C) Against measurement noise, 250 steps: section map by least squares and by IV, phase-indexed maps, and 8-sector piecewise-linear maps. (D) Piecewise-linear maps against the number of sectors composed over one step, 250 steps.](figures/Figure_03){#fig-floquet-maps fig-alt="Four panels: return-map eigenvalues in the complex plane, estimated spectral radius against record length, against measurement noise, and against the number of piecewise sectors."}

The instrumental-variable correction is a constructive result: under the tested assumptions, linear-map estimation allows a substantial noise bias to be corrected [@dawson2016; @hemati2017; @askham2018]. It does not make the multiplier a complete description of recovery. Together, the conceptual and estimation challenges motivate models that can answer richer questions about the evolving response.

## What should a useful model of gait dynamics provide?

Replacing one stability estimate with a more complicated model helps only if the model answers questions the estimate cannot. We want a model of the gait pattern and the evolution of departures from it: disturbances, compensatory coordination, and recovery considered together. This does not require claiming to reconstruct every physiological mechanism from kinematics.

### The capabilities that matter

1. **Forecast the response to disturbances (R1).** From an observed state, predict how the deviation from the usual cycle evolves over the following strides, including its size, direction, timing, and return, more accurately than reference forecasts such as the mean cycle. This applies to ordinary walking, whose deviations are themselves responses to ongoing disturbances (@fig-transient), and to larger disturbances of the kinds represented in the training data. Assess timing errors separately from errors in amplitude and coordination.
2. **Remain credible beyond a short fitted segment (R2).** Produce plausible sustained walking and bounded trajectories over the intended observation window. A good short fit alone is insufficient.
3. **Give reproducible answers (R3).** Conclusions about a person or condition should not depend strongly on arbitrary fitting initializations.
4. **Work with realistic recordings (R4).** Establish sensitivity to noise, record length, partial observation, and available excitation, and make uncertainty and data requirements visible. A model that works on real data must also be practical to fit and validate on it, without prohibitive computation or opaque tuning.
5. **Expose interpretable dynamical structure (R5).** Allow examination of how disturbances spread between movements, where amplification occurs, and which responses dominate.
6. **Support comparison across people and conditions (R6).** Fitted models should share a structure in which the same quantities can be computed and compared between participants, conditions, and tasks, so that differences reflect the dynamics rather than the fit.

### What data are needed to meet those requirements?

Repeated similar strides can describe the usual gait pattern well while revealing little about responses to substantial disturbances. Systems can share a periodic orbit yet differ away from it. Passive recordings may contain informative deviations, but their adequacy must be demonstrated for the particular response being claimed.

Human gait recordings show the problem directly. In 299 treadmill trials of 15 s, most of each trial's variance lies in the mean cycle, and the deviations that carry the response to disturbances are a small remainder (@fig-gait-mean A–B). Whole-trajectory operator measures can inherit that structure: much of the companion paper's transient-growth signature at a one-third-stride window is reproduced by the mean cycle alone (@fig-gait-mean C–D). This does not make the waveform unimportant; it limits what such a signature alone establishes about recovery, and it means a model can fit a recording closely while learning little about its deviations.

(A) One able-bodied trial (14 strides at 124 cm/s): knee angle of every stride (grey) and the mean cycle (black); below, each stride's deviation from the mean cycle. (C) Transient growth (TG) of the companion paper's operator [@hess2026nonnormality] (delay DMD, rank 70, ridge 10^−4^, stride-rescaled time; TG = max over one stride of ‖Ãᵏ‖) against the delay window: recorded trials (solid) and each trial's mean cycle repeated with no deviations (dashed); medians. The data must therefore cover excursions relevant to the intended question. Training and validation should include appropriate disturbance directions, phases, and magnitudes, with independent cases reserved for testing. A forecast that begins at the disturbance also poses a different task from one initialized after observing part of the recovery. We distinguish these protocols explicitly below.

Record length, measurement quality, unobserved state, and contact events further constrain what can be learned. These are practical considerations in building a useful model, not reasons to abandon the modeling question. The appropriate test is whether the fitted model predicts relevant responses beyond simple reference forecasts and whether that conclusion survives independent data.

## How well do existing modeling approaches meet those needs?

We compare Hankel-DMD, a linear operator on histories of measurements [@brunton2017; @kutz2016], with an echo state network (ESN) [@jaeger2001], a neural ODE [@chen2018], and a spectral-submanifold model [@haller2016; @cenedese2022]. Their flexibility, fitting procedures, and computational demands differ. The experiments assess those practical differences; they are not a proof that one model class is universally superior. We do not compare transformers [@vaswani2017]. They forecast from a finite window of past observations rather than evolving a state, so they offer no vector field, cycle, or linearization to examine, and they typically need far more data than individual gait recordings provide. They can be useful forecasters, but they are not dynamical models in the sense required here.

### Can they reproduce and sustain walking?

Predictions are evaluated by autonomous rollout: after initialization, no further observations are supplied. Reference forecasts repeat a phase-aligned mean cycle or the last stride, establishing what fitted dynamics add. We report performance on both the full movement signal and departures from the mean cycle, because the usual gait pattern accounts for most variance in the tested human recordings.

Validation should resemble the intended use. Across the benchmark's DMD and ESN tuning grids, rollout-validation errors rank settings by their test forecast error more reliably than one-step errors (median rank correlations 0.71–0.88 versus −0.19 to 0.40). Several held-out starts provide a useful check against settings that fit locally but fail when run freely (@suppfig-validation). Tuning effort was unequal across model classes: DMD and ESN used rollout-based parameter searches, the neural ODE used a fixed recipe, and SSMLearnPy used a configuration tuned on gait.

Grey, held-out data; colour, free runs of every seed (ESN, neural ODE), polynomial degree (SSMLearnPy) or rank (DMD), overlaid; runs that leave the frame are cut. Labels give the outcome counts after 30 cycles. (B) Outcome after 30 free-running cycles, pooled over systems and both regimes; Hankel-DMD as tuned (with the spectral constraint the training data selected, usually placing persistent modes on the unit circle) and tuned by the same training-data criterion with no constraint. (C) Forecast error over the first held-out cycle per system (realistic and long regimes); black bars, the mean-cycle reference forecast, which defines zero skill; points at 10 diverged. (D) Share of free runs remaining within ε = 0.5 cycle SD (RMS over channels) of the true cycle over the eight stored cycles: for the simulated systems, the noise-free cycle; for SLIP, its settled cycle; for gait, where no true cycle is known, the states observed in training. Shading, 95% bootstrap intervals over the 13 cells; dashed, DMD retuned without a constraint. The held-out data stay within 0.32 of the same references. DMD and ESN hyperparameters were chosen on the training data only (fitted on all but the last two training cycles, selected by free-run error on those); the neural ODE uses one fixed recipe; SSMLearnPy the configuration tuned on gait.](figures/Figure_05){#fig-selfdriving fig-alt="Grid of phase portraits of free runs for four model classes on five systems, a bar chart of outcomes after 30 cycles, and first-cycle errors with a mean-cycle reference level."}

With clean training data, DMD and ESN often predict the first held-out cycle closely. With noisy data, the ESN outperforms DMD in some settings but fails substantially in others; DMD is more consistent in this benchmark. Sustained behavior is a separate requirement: the DMD fits maintain the correct cycle in 92% of system–regime cells, compared with 42–62% for the other tested approaches (@fig-selfdriving B). This does not depend on the spectral constraint. Tuned without any constraint, DMD also keeps the cycle in 12 of 13 cells and never blows up; removing the constraint from the selected fits leaves 11 of 13, the other two decaying slowly. A stricter test asks how long each free run stays close to the true cycle. Within half a cycle standard deviation of it, about twice the largest departure of the held-out data, 92% of the DMD runs remain for all eight stored cycles, against 58–65% for the other model classes (@fig-selfdriving D); within a quarter of a standard deviation, 62% against 50–56%. These percentages describe the tested configurations, not intrinsic guarantees, and staying near the cycle does not establish correct perturbation dynamics.

### Can they forecast the short-time response?

Because walking is disturbed at every step (@fig-transient), its future contains a predictable part, the response to disturbances already received, and an unpredictable part, the responses to disturbances still to come. No model can forecast the second. We therefore test forecasts on the kicked SLIP walker of @fig-transient A, where the predictable part is known exactly: the noise-free continuation of the true state, which sets a ceiling on attainable skill (@fig-predictable). Models are trained on 60 steps (about 30 strides, comparable to two 15-s gait recordings) or 300 steps of one walk, observed with 1% measurement noise in stride-normalized time, and their settings are chosen by multistart rollout error on an independent walk. From 300 starts at random phases in ten held-out walks, each forecast is warmed up on four strides of observations and runs freely for three strides. Skill is scored against what actually happened, relative to the mean-cycle reference forecast.

The predictable horizon is short. With speed feedback, the ceiling falls from a skill of 0.73 over the first stride to 0.32 over the next two, because most of the later deviation comes from disturbances that have not yet occurred. Both models forecast most of the attainable skill in the first stride: with the full centre-of-mass state and 60 training steps, 82% for Hankel-DMD and 89% for the ESN, whose four seeds agree closely. Beyond the first stride the ESN retains more (63% against 27% of the attainable skill), and with 300 training steps both approach the ceiling (ESN 93%, DMD 86%). Open loop, where disturbances decay more slowly and more of the future is predictable, the two are similar. Observing only the height separates them: the ESN stays close to the ceiling, whereas DMD falls below the mean-cycle reference after about one and a half strides. No forecast diverged.

Forecasting the short-time response is therefore achievable for both model classes when the state is well observed, and in this test the ESN is the more accurate forecaster at longer horizons and under partial observation.

(C) Open loop (ρ = 0.95 per step), full state. (D) With feedback, height only. Shading, the first stride.](figures/Figure_06){#fig-predictable fig-alt="One SLIP forecast with the true future and its predictable part, and forecast skill against horizon for Hankel-DMD, an ESN, persistence and the ceiling under feedback, open loop and height-only observation."}

Larger disturbances are harder (@suppfig-large-kicks). After kicks of about one cycle SD to a pair of coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo oscillators, the ESN forecast the fast return of the cycle's amplitude almost exactly, whereas DMD carried a waveform error, and neither predicted the slow recovery of the coordination between the two oscillators. A model that is linear in delay coordinates approximates a cycle's phase and decaying modes well only near the cycle; far from it, part of a kick is attributed to the cycle's own harmonics and persists. Large deviations are therefore where nonlinear models are needed, and the case for linear models cannot rest on forecast accuracy alone. Earlier single-disturbance experiments with small kicks are also in the supplement (@suppfig-small-kicks).
### Modeling the response instead of the whole system

Every model above was fitted to the whole recorded signal, so it had to reproduce the cycle and the response to disturbances at once. In gait the two differ greatly in size: deviations from the average stride are a few percent of the joint-angle range (@fig-gait-mean), so a cycle error of a fraction of a percent, in waveform or timing, is as large as the response itself. The alternative is to supply the cycle, as a phase and an average stride, and to model only the deviation from it. Near a stable cycle, deviations evolve linearly with a dynamics that repeats every cycle (Floquet theory), so the natural model is linear with a matrix that varies with phase, as in phase-varying models of human gait [@revzen2012; @rosenberg2020].

We compared the two approaches on long treadmill running recordings, where data are plentiful: 22 trials of about 320 strides from four people [@maus2015]. Phase was taken from the two leading principal components of a half-stride window of all joint angles, strides were resampled to 100 samples, and the deviation was measured from a 61-stride moving-average stride (@suppfig-running-method). Modeling the whole signal forfeited most of the forecastable response (@fig-running A). With 150 training strides and one eighth of a stride ahead, the best whole-signal model reached $R^2$ = 0.17 in real time (the phase-varying linear model, with the phase extrapolated at the previous stride's rate), against 0.68 for the same model class fitted to the deviation; a quarter of a stride ahead, every whole-signal model was worse than the average stride. That reference knows when each future stride begins; an average stride advanced at the previous stride's rate, which a real-time forecast could use, scored far lower ($R^2$ = −3.2), so the whole-signal models did predict the timing. Their difficulty is the size of the response: deviations from the average stride were 0.9% of the signal's variance, so a whole-signal DMD forecast with $R^2$ = 0.986 on the raw joint angles still had an error larger than the deviation it was meant to forecast. Supplying the timing, by resampling strides between their actual boundaries, recovered part of the gap for the phase-varying model (0.36) and for DMD, but not for the ESN; supplying the cycle as well recovered the rest for all three. Part of the deviation's advantage is information about slow drift: the average stride is a moving average over strides on both sides of the forecast, which a causal estimate would have to approximate.

Modeled as a deviation, the response was learnable with enough strides, and a linear model with phase-dependent matrices learned it best (@fig-running B). Forecasting one eighth of a stride ahead, its median $R^2$ rose from 0.28 with 16 training strides to 0.41 with 32 and 0.68 with 150, against 0.45 for an ESN given the same phase information and 0.38 for a time-invariant linear model, which stopped improving after about 32 strides. Phase dependence has to be estimated economically: a phase-binned model of the same family [@rosenberg2020], which divides the data among 20 phase bins, reached only 0.15 with 32 strides and caught up only near 64. Representing the matrices as smooth functions of phase shares information across the stride. A 15-s walking trial, about 9–15 strides, lies where every model is weak ($R^2 \le 0.28$ one eighth of a stride ahead and below zero at a quarter), which explains why no model forecast the 15-s gait trials better than the mean cycle. Added measurement noise narrowed the phase-varying model's lead; at noise equal to the deviation's own spread it matched the ESN (@fig-running C). A lattice-constrained model, which imposes the cycle and a single decaying mode, did not forecast the running deviations ($R^2 \le 0.06$).

![**Modeling the deviation from the cycle, rather than the whole signal, makes the short-time response of human running learnable; a linear model with phase-dependent matrices learns it best.** Long treadmill running recordings [@maus2015], 22 trials of about 320 strides (4 people), six sagittal joint angles. Strides cut at the phase of the leading oscillatory pair of all angles and resampled to 100 samples; deviation from a 61-stride moving-average stride (@suppfig-running-method). Score: $R^2$ of the deviation, i.e. skill against the average stride at each sample's actual phase; medians and interquartile ranges over trials. (D) The deviation against the forecast horizon, 150 training strides.](figures/Figure_07){#fig-running fig-alt="Forecast skill for running deviations: whole signal against deviation representations, learning curves by training strides, the effect of added noise and the decline with forecast horizon, for phase-varying, phase-binned and time-invariant linear models, a lattice model and an ESN."}

### Can one model serve many recordings?

Pooling recordings into one model is attractive when each recording is short, and it is how recurrent models of gait are usually trained [@winner2023]. Whether pooling helps depends on how different the recordings are relative to how variable each one is. We measured this as a heterogeneity ratio $H$: in the pool's shared delay embedding, the typical distance from the states of one recording to the nearest states of another, divided by the same distance between two halves of one recording. $H \approx 1$ means that two recordings are as alike as two halves of the same one, so pooling only adds data (@fig-heterogeneity).

Pooling paid only at low heterogeneity. Over 187 pools of 2–299 gait trials, a single DMD fitted to the pool forecast its own trials better than per-trial fits in 55% of pools with $H < 1.5$, and in 2% of pools above it. At high heterogeneity, small pools were nearly harmless and large pools were not: one linear operator can hold a few distinct cycles side by side, but not many. A trial left out of the pool was forecast worse than by its own fit at every heterogeneity. The two simulated cohorts, whose individuals differ slightly, lie at $H$ = 1.0 and 1.7 and gained slightly from pooling. The 299 gait trials, from 42 people at different speeds, lie at $H$ = 9.1. A group fit to all of them failed for every model class (median first-cycle skill: DMD −4.0, ESN −6.9, LSTM −3.0, against −0.12, −0.86 and −0.14 for per-trial fits). Recordings of human gait therefore call for per-person, and often per-condition, models whose quantities can be compared (R6), rather than one model of everyone.

![**One model for many recordings helps only when they are nearly alike.** Heterogeneity $H$: in a pool's shared delay embedding (delays spanning one cycle, leading principal components), the median over pairs of recordings of the mean distance from the states of one to the nearest states of the other, divided by the same distance between two halves of one recording. Gait: 187 pools of the 299 trials (nearest neighbours, one participant, one speed band, random draws, participant groups and all trials); one Hankel-DMD fitted to each pool's training windows (settings chosen on held-back cycles), against each trial's own fit; first-cycle skill against the mean-cycle reference. Hexagons, the simulated SLIP and coupled-FHN cohorts (10 individuals each). (A) Group minus individual skill for the pool's own trials, median over the pool. (B) The same for a trial left out of the pool's fit. (C) Pool size against heterogeneity, median gain in each cell; white, no such pools in the data.](figures/Figure_08){#fig-heterogeneity fig-alt="Group-minus-individual forecast skill against a heterogeneity ratio for pools of gait trials and two simulated cohorts, for pooled and held-out trials, and a map of pool size against heterogeneity."}

### What is the overall comparison?

The requirements should be considered together (@tbl-scorecard). The ESN's closer forecasts of the short-time response, especially from partial observations, are an important success. DMD's appeal lies in the combination of consistent benchmark forecasts, reproducible fitting at fixed settings, explicit constraints, and accessible analysis. Neither result removes the need to validate the response relevant to a particular application.

| Requirement | Neural ODE | ESN | SSMLearnPy | Hankel-DMD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 first-cycle skill, clean / noisy benchmark | −3.5 to −0.1 / −3.4 to −0.1 | +0.7 to +1.0 / −13 to +0.4 | −73 to +0.4 / −4.5 to 0 | +0.6 to +1.0 / −0.4 to +0.2 |
| R1 share of attainable skill, first stride / strides 1–3, SLIP with feedback (full state; height only) | not tested | 89% / 63% (98% / 77%) | not tested | 82% / 27% (85% / −49%) |
| R2 correct cycle / blow-up after 30 cycles, benchmark | 42% / 12% | 60% / 19% | 62% / 12% | 92% / 0% |
| R3 reproducibility | seed-dependent | seed-dependent | not tested | unique ridge fit at fixed coordinates/settings |
| R4 realistic recordings: noise, data, partial observation, cost per fit | experiment-dependent; hours per fit | near the ceiling with partial observation; not systematically timed | not established; not systematically timed | some linear-map noise biases correctable; multi-stride forecasts need a well-observed state or more data; seconds per fit |
| R5 response structure | requires analysis of fitted field | requires analysis of fitted reservoir | reduced dynamical representation | explicit propagation and response operators |
| R6 comparability across people and conditions | fitted field differs by seed | reservoir differs by seed | manifold coordinates fitted per data set | shared delay coordinates and operator quantities at fixed settings; not yet tested across people |

: **Practical strengths and limits across the model requirements.** First-cycle skill is 1 − model error / mean-cycle-reference error, from @fig-selfdriving; clean and noisy regimes use different training lengths. Share of attainable skill is model skill divided by the skill of the noise-free continuation over each horizon, with 60 training steps (@fig-predictable); ESN values are medians over four seeds. These are separate experiments and their error measures should not be compared numerically. Sustained-behavior percentages refer to the benchmark's tuned fits; unconstrained DMD gives the same 92%. R5 describes available model structure, not validated physiological interpretation. {#tbl-scorecard}

## Why linear models are a strong foundation for this broader goal

“Linear” does not require the measured gait waveform to be sinusoidal or the underlying neuromechanics to be linear. A model can evolve linearly in an expanded representation, such as a history of movements, while reconstructing rich oscillatory signals. Choosing and validating that representation remains part of the modeling problem.

Most interpretable analyses of a nonlinear model also pass through a linearization. Floquet multipliers of a neural ODE or reservoir, response directions of a recurrent network, and transient growth of any fitted model are computed from Jacobians along the model's own cycle, which must first be located and is itself an estimate (@suppfig-floquet-models). A model that is linear in suitable coordinates provides these quantities directly. Linear phase-varying models have also predicted kinematic responses to ankle exoskeletons about as accurately as nonlinear phase-varying models [@rosenberg2020]. Linear models are therefore worth considering first, with nonlinear models adopted where their validated predictions are better.

### They make fitting and model checking tractable

For fixed delay coordinates, rank, and positive ridge regularization, linear regression has a unique solution and does not depend on an optimization seed. This supports repeatable comparisons and makes cross-validation and resampling practical. It does not eliminate choices about representation or establish that the data uniquely identify the physical system.

An explicit operator also makes assumptions inspectable. Spectral constraints can enforce desired sustained behavior directly, although the benchmark fits rarely needed them (@fig-selfdriving B). Measurement-noise bias can sometimes be analyzed and corrected, as in the earlier SLIP return-map comparison (@fig-floquet-maps) [@dawson2016; @hemati2017; @askham2018]. The correction depends on the instrument assumptions and can be variable in short records.

These advantages coexist with limitations. A delay model may reproduce a cycle while retaining an amplitude or waveform error, and it may fail to predict a large recovery despite relevant training examples (@suppfig-large-kicks). Its multi-stride forecasts also degrade when the state is only partly observed (@fig-predictable D). Linear models should be favored for the requirements they meet, with nonlinear alternatives retained when their validated predictions are better.

### They let us ask richer questions about the response

The companion work motivates examining non-normality and response structure beyond the spectrum [@hess2026nonnormality]. In a validated linear model, these tools address complementary questions:

- **Transient growth:** which disturbances produce the largest excursions over a specified number of strides, and when?
- **Response directions and coordination:** which combinations of movements are amplified, and where does the response appear?
- **Resolvent gains:** which temporal patterns of repeated forcing produce large responses for the specified inputs and outputs?
- **Pseudospectra:** how sensitive are spectral conclusions to changes or uncertainty in the fitted operator?

These quantities require a defined state, norm, perturbation, and observation. Amplification of a whole delay history is not automatically amplification of an instantaneous physical kick. Likewise, an undamped resolvent can be singular at a neutral mode; a model with modes placed on the unit circle needs an explicit evaluation convention. The present manuscript motivates these analyses as capabilities of linear models; it does not yet establish a new validated physical-response result from the pending resolvent experiment.

The aim is a connected description of gait response: prediction, amplification, coordination, and sensitivity considered together. Physical meaning comes from the chosen inputs and outputs and from agreement with independent responses, not simply from having a matrix to analyze.

## What does this mean for human gait studies?

Return to the questions of response and recovery. A model fitted to ordinary walking may characterize a person's usual movement pattern very well while providing little evidence about a substantial disturbance. What it establishes must be distinguished from what requires informative perturbations or changes in task.

As shown earlier, the usual gait pattern dominates the tested recordings and can dominate whole-trajectory operator measures (@fig-gait-mean).


The mean cycle also identifies individuals at least as well as the tested operator signature (@suppfig-identification). Distinguishing people is therefore not equivalent to identifying their response dynamics. In the tested 15-second recordings and out-of-trial evaluations, the examined linear models do not predict the next stride's deviation better than the mean-stride reference (@suppfig-lattice). This is a result about these data and analyses, not a universal statement that human gait is unpredictable.

Known cycle structure can be imposed on a linear model [@kvalheim2021]. The lattice-constrained SLIP example shows how that structure can help organize recovery, while the human-data comparison shows that imposing structure does not create predictive information absent from the tested recordings (@suppfig-lattice).

Models fitted during active walking describe the combined observed mechanics and control. Attributing their responses to a physiological mechanism, or separating feedback from the mechanical plant, requires additional experimental information. Applications should therefore be posed as testable questions: whether a response feature differs between people or conditions, changes with training, a device, or impairment, or predicts recovery during an independent perturbation task.

## Conclusion

The goal is to understand and predict how walking responds, compensates, and recovers. Asymptotic stability contributes to that description but is not an adequate primary target on its own. Models should be judged by their ability to predict relevant responses, sustain credible behavior, provide reproducible and interpretable estimates, work within practical recording and computational constraints, and support comparison across people and conditions.

Across these requirements, linear models offer a strong foundation for studying gait dynamics. Their value lies in the combination of tractable fitting, explicit assumptions, and tools for examining the response. That promise must be realized through appropriate experiments and independent validation, including recognition of cases where nonlinear models predict recovery better.

The gait recordings analysed here are openly available through the dataset described by @winner2023.

## Code accessibility

All code used for simulations, model fitting and figure generation is available at [github.com/michaelhess17/Gait_Modeling_Perspective_Paper](https://github.com/michaelhess17/Gait_Modeling_Perspective_Paper). Each figure is drawn by its own script from cached results, `scripts/figures/Figure_NN.jl` (supplementary figures `Figure_SNN.jl`); `julia --project=. scripts/make_figures.jl` rebuilds them all. The analyses that produce the caches, and the order in which to run them, are listed in `scripts/README.md`:

- @fig-schematic: `Figure_01.jl` (exact linear examples, no data)
- @fig-transient: `Figure_02.jl`, from `fig1_transient_data.jl`, `slip_truth.jl`, `systems_truth.jl`
- @fig-floquet-maps: `Figure_03.jl`, from `fig3_slip_maps.jl`, `slip_truth.jl`
- @fig-gait-mean: `Figure_04.jl`, from `fig5_gait_data.jl`
- @fig-selfdriving: `Figure_05.jl`, from `self_driving_benchmark.jl`, `dmd_tuning.jl`, `esn_tuning.jl`, `ssm_self_driving.py`, `stabilization_benchmark.jl`, `r2_tube.jl`
- @fig-predictable: `Figure_06.jl`, from `slip_predictable_truth.jl` (SLIP.jl environment) and `predictable_response.jl`
- @fig-running: `Figure_07.jl`, from `maus_extract.jl`, `maus_learning_all.jl`, `maus_ladder.jl`
- @fig-heterogeneity: `Figure_08.jl`, from `gait_group_fits.jl`, `heterogeneity_pools.jl`, `cohort_fits.jl`, `slip_family_data.jl`, `cfhn_family_data.jl`
- Supplementary figures S1–S11: `Figure_S01.jl` … `Figure_S11.jl`; their analyses are listed in `scripts/README.md`

Results reported in the text without a figure: `gait_group_fits.jl` (individual against group fits on all gait trials), `cohort_fits.jl` (the same on the simulated cohorts), `large_kicks_dmd_probe.jl` and `cfhn_density_probe.jl` (DMD on coupled FHN: cycle harmonics, noise, training size), `iv_gait_stride.jl`, `iv_gait_operator.jl`, `fig6_bias_correction.jl`, `dmd_noise_variants.jl`, `floquet_tuned.jl` and `coupling_benchmark.jl`.

::: {#suppfig-validation}
![](figures/Figure_S02){fig-alt="Rank correlations between four validation errors and test forecast error for DMD and ESN settings, and the test forecast skill of the setting each criterion chooses."}

**Validate by rollout, not by one-step error.** Every setting of the benchmark's tuning grids (Hankel-DMD, 60 settings of delay depth × rank × variant; ESN, 36 settings × 3 seeds) in each of the 13 system–regime cells, fitted on the training window minus its last two cycles and scored on those two cycles by in-sample one-step error (a training loss), held-out one-step (teacher-forced) error, one held-out rollout from the end of the fitting data, and the mean of 1-cycle rollouts from 5 starts across the held-out cycles (multistart); then refitted on the full training window and run freely. (A) Rank correlation across settings between each validation error and the test forecast error over the first held-out cycle, one dot per cell; bars, medians. (B) Test forecast skill (1 − error / error of the mean-cycle reference forecast) of the setting each criterion would choose, one dot per cell (open, below −3); best on test, the setting with the lowest test error. Numbers: cells in which the chosen setting keeps the right cycle over 30 cycles.
:::

::: {#suppfig-large-kicks}
![](figures/Figure_S03){fig-alt="Example forecasts after an amplitude kick and a coordination kick in coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillators, and forecast error and recovery over cycles for Hankel-DMD and an ESN across all held-out kicks."}

**Large kicks: fitted models forecast the fast return of the cycle's amplitude, but not the slow recovery of coordination.** Two coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo oscillators in a smooth regime ($\varepsilon = 0.25$, coupling 0.025), no measurement or process noise. Training: 24 sequences, each two undisturbed cycles and eight cycles after a kick of 0.4–1.6 cycle SD (RMS per coordinate), half along the cycle's amplitude (both oscillators displaced alike) and half against the coordination (displaced in opposite directions); settings chosen by five-cycle rollout error on eight further sequences. Both models also observe the standardized coordination signal $w_1 - w_2$; the imposed jump is excluded from DMD's and the ESN's regression targets. Test: 16 held-out kicks, four phases × two sizes (0.8, 1.3 SD) × two kinds. Forecasts start from two cycles of history ending in the kicked state and run for 12 cycles with no later observations. (A, B) One kick of each kind, 1.3 SD, chosen by the truth's excursion before any model was fitted: $v_1$ (A) and $w_1 - w_2$ (B). Dashed black, truth; blue, Hankel-DMD; orange, the ESN's four seeds. (C, D) Forecast error per cycle after the kick (RMS distance from the true state, in training SD), median and interquartile range over the 8 held-out kicks of each kind (the ESN: median over seeds first). Dotted grey, the forecast that the kick changed nothing (the unkicked continuation). (E) Coordination kicks: RMS distance to the true limit cycle per cycle, for the truth (dashed) and each model's forecast; the distance ignores timing, so it measures predicted recovery alone.
:::

::: {#suppfig-small-kicks}
![](figures/Figure_S04){fig-alt="Earlier small-perturbation recovery comparisons for coupled FHN and SLIP, and fitted SLIP multipliers."}

**Predicting the return to the true cycle from real perturbed states, and what each model's own cycle has learned (R1, R3).** Models trained on the same 10 decays × 3 cycles were warmed up on the true perturbed trajectory and run freely. Deviation = distance to the curve through the true cycle's samples, RMS over each cycle after the warm-up, for model and truth alike; median over 4 starts, kicked at 4 phases of the cycle. Black, truth; one line per fit: Hankel-DMD is one least-squares fit, the ESN 4 seeds and the neural ODE 3 seeds at fixed tuned settings. Triangles, distance of each fit's settled cycle from the true cycle, below which its deviation cannot fall. (A) Coupled FHN, per cycle: the truth returns at 0.69 per cycle, but every model's cycle is displaced from the true cycle by as much as the perturbation, so distance to the true cycle includes persistent waveform and coordination errors. (B) SLIP, centre-of-mass state (y, ẋ, ẏ), per step: the perturbation is larger than the models' cycle offsets, and every model tracks the return. (C) SLIP: multipliers of each model's own cycle, rotation against modulus per step. DMD, eigenvalues of its operator in the cycle frame (rotation from the nearest harmonic); square, the one next to the 8th harmonic; ESN, the leading eigenvalue of the monodromy of its own settled cycle (closed-loop Jacobians chained over one period, phase eigenvalue removed), one per seed; star, the exact multiplier (0.769 ∠ 13.6°); diamond, the lattice-constrained fit (@suppfig-lattice).

This earlier experiment uses a sharper FHN regime ($\varepsilon = 0.08$, coupling 0.02) and observes 170 post-perturbation samples before autonomous prediction. It is distinct from the smoother, immediate-kick experiment in @suppfig-large-kicks. Small difference signals are sensitive to timing discrepancies; the FHN result does not establish that the model classes cannot learn recovery.
:::

::: {#suppfig-running-method}
![](figures/Figure_S05){fig-alt="Six joint angles of a running trial with stride boundaries, the loop of the two leading principal components that defines the phase, strides with their average, the deviation with its state window, responses of the same deviation started at four phases, and one forecast."}

**How the phase-varying linear model of running deviations is built, on one trial** [@maus2015]. (A) Six sagittal joint angles (standardised) and the stride boundaries. (B) The phase: the two leading principal components of a half-stride window of all angles trace a loop, and the phase θ is the angle around it; a stride ends each time θ completes a turn (unlike the Hilbert phase of one joint, this does not pin any channel at the cut). (C) Every stride resampled to 100 samples; the average stride is a 61-stride moving average. (D) What is modelled: the deviation from that average stride; its state z is the last 8 samples. (E) The model, z~t+1~ = A(θ~t~) z~t~ with A(θ) a Fourier series in θ (up to 8 harmonics), fitted by one ridge regression of z~t+1~ on [z~t~, cos θ~t~·z~t~, sin θ~t~·z~t~, …]: the same knee deviation evolves differently depending on where in the stride it starts. With no harmonics the model is time-invariant DMD of the deviation. (F) One forecast from a held-out stride, with strides 1–150 fitted.
:::

::: {#suppfig-floquet-models}
![](figures/Figure_S06){fig-alt="Floquet multipliers read out of neural ODEs, ESNs and DMD against the known truth for several systems and data regimes."}

**Floquet multipliers read out of fitted models, against known truth.** For each system and data regime, the transverse multiplier is read from the model's own limit cycle by chaining one-step Jacobians over one period (neural ODE, ESN), or by a variational probe on data-delay windows (Hankel-DMD, coupled FHN only). Neural ODE, 4 seeds on one data set; ESN, 8 seeds on one data set plus one ESN per data realisation (10); DMD, 8 analysis settings (window ½ or 1 cycle × rank 16, 30, 50, 80; least squares) × 10 data realisations. Points are drawn only for runs that settled on a cycle; runs that collapsed or whose period is more than 10% off the data period are marked.
:::

::: {#suppfig-identification}
![](figures/Figure_S07){fig-alt="Identification accuracy of individuals from different gait feature families, with chance level."}

**Identifying individuals: the mean cycle does as well as the operator signature.** The companion paper's split-half protocol: each person's trials are split at random into halves, features are averaged per half and z-scored against the able-bodied half-A distribution, and a person is identified when their other half is the nearest (cosine) match among all 42 people. Mean and 95% range over 200 random splits; dashed, chance (1/42). Deviation features can carry within-stride timing jitter and marker artefacts.
:::

::: {#suppfig-lattice}
![](figures/Figure_S08){fig-alt="The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay, Koopman spectra of the lattice and Hankel-DMD, SLIP off-cycle metrics for all models, gait forecast skill, forecast error against assumed multiplier, and skill under different selection rules."}

**Imposing the limit cycle's structure on a linear model.** (A) The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay: state = fitted cycle a(θ) plus one Floquet mode Re[ψ e^μt^ b(θ)]; the phase advances uniformly, the mode shrinks by the multiplier and turns by its rotation every step, and its shape b(θ) repeats every step. (B) A stable limit cycle's Koopman spectrum is a lattice: read relative to the nearest harmonic, every harmonic sits at (0°, 1) and every Floquet sideband at the star. Hankel-DMD (same 10 three-step decays) fits each eigenvalue on its own; the lattice fit returns one value. (C) SLIP off-cycle metrics, 4 starts: |error| of the 4-step relaxation rate (the metric of @suppfig-small-kicks, before its scoring was corrected) and distance to the true cycle after 25 steps relative to the initial distance. (D) Human gait and kicked SLIP walks: R² of the deviation from the mean stride 1 stride ahead (filled; 2 strides ahead, open) from half a stride of data; median and interquartile range over trials; multiplier and DMD rank chosen on the person's other trials. (E) Forecast error over strides +1 and +2 against the assumed multiplier modulus: kicked SLIP walks have a minimum near the truth; gait profiles are flat at the mean stride's error. (F) Lattice skill with the multiplier chosen out of trial (solid), on the scored strides (dashed), and on stride-shuffled copies of each trial (dotted): on gait about half of the on-test skill is selection, and the rest does not carry over to other trials.
:::

**Forecast skill on held-out gait.** Every method gets the same information (z-scored joint angles up to sample 1000 of each 15-s trial) and is scored on the same held-out targets by the instantaneous RMSE across the six channels. (A) Median error against lead time for the tuned SSMLearnPy delay map and a rank-70 Hankel-DMD (ridge 10^−4^, stabilised; the companion paper's settings), with two reference forecasts that need no dynamics and define zero skill: repeating a phase-aligned mean training cycle (phase template) and repeating the last stride; interquartile range shaded for the template and the SSM. (B) Per trial at 2.7 s lead: SSMLearnPy error against the mean-cycle reference's. (C–E) Knee angle in one representative trial per group.

::: {#suppfig-node-gait}
![](figures/Figure_S10){fig-alt="Hip-knee diagrams of neural-ODE forecasts for three trials, forecast error against lead time, and learned period and multiplier against training loss."}

**Neural ODEs on real gait: a good fit, an unconstrained dynamics.** A deliberately over-parameterised neural ODE (3 × 128, about 35,000 parameters against 3,000 training values), trained by multiple shooting on 10 s of six z-scored joint angles from one trial per group, six random seeds each. (A–C) Hip–knee angle–angle diagrams (limb 1): grey, training strides; black, the held-out 5 s; colour, each seed's autonomous forecast from the last training sample. (D) Forecast error against lead time for every seed, with the phase-aligned mean-cycle template for reference. (E) Period of the cycle each learned field settles onto, relative to the measured stride period, against the validation error of the autonomous forecast over the held-out 5 s. (F) Transverse Floquet multiplier of that cycle against the same validation error: held-out forecasts do not pin the dynamics.

::: {#suppfig-offcycle}
![](figures/Figure_S11){fig-alt="Deviation from each model's own attractor against cycles after an off-cycle start, for DMD, ESN and neural-ODE fits and the truth."}

**Off-cycle relaxation of models trained on decays from perturbed starts.** The true system is started off its cycle; each model, warmed up on 170 samples of that trajectory, then runs freely. Deviation is the distance to the nearest point of the model's own attractor (independent of phase), RMS over each cycle, relative to the first cycle; for the truth, the distance to the true cycle, which decays by the multiplier every cycle. One line per fitted model (DMD, tuned setting; ESN and neural ODE, one line per seed), median over 4 start phases; runs that blew up are not drawn.
